Concept comparison

Stretch vs Shear

Both preserve area. Both appear in $SL(2,\mathbb R)$. They differ in how many eigen-directions they have — and that one difference changes everything.

Stretch hyperbolic type — two independent eigen-directions

The matrix is diagonal — two entries, two jobs, no mixing:

$$ A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} $$

The top-left $2$ acts only on the $x$-component; the bottom-right $\tfrac12$ acts only on the $y$-component. They are completely independent. Multiply out to see it directly:

$$ Ae_1 = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\0\end{bmatrix} = 2\,e_1 $$

The $x$-axis comes out pointing the same way but twice as long. $\lambda_1=2$ is the scale factor — literally the ratio of output length to input length along that direction.

$$ Ae_2 = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0\\\tfrac12\end{bmatrix} = \tfrac12\,e_2 $$

The $y$-axis comes out pointing the same way but half as long. $\lambda_2=\tfrac12$ is the scale factor there.

For any vector $\mathbf v = \alpha e_1 + \beta e_2$:

$$ A\mathbf v = 2\alpha\,e_1 + \tfrac12\beta\,e_2. $$

Each component scales by its own eigenvalue, completely independently. The $x$-component never talks to the $y$-component. This is the hallmark of a machine with two independent eigen-directions.

Area: $\det A = 2\times\tfrac12=1$. Stretch by $2$ in one direction, shrink by $\tfrac12$ in the other — the two effects cancel perfectly. This is why $A\in SL(2,\mathbb R)$.

Faint circle = input. Solid ellipse = output. Green arrow = $Ae_1$ (doubled); sienna arrow = $Ae_2$ (halved).
Complete picture
Eigenvalues: $\lambda_1=2$ (stretch), $\lambda_2=\tfrac12$ (shrink). Two distinct real values — the signature of the hyperbolic case.
Eigenvectors: $e_1=(1,0)^T$ for $\lambda_1$ and $e_2=(0,1)^T$ for $\lambda_2$. Two independent directions. For a diagonal matrix these are always the coordinate axes — readable by inspection.
What the unit circle does: becomes an axis-aligned ellipse with semi-axes $2$ (horizontal) and $\tfrac12$ (vertical). Area = $2\times\tfrac12\times\pi=\pi$. Unchanged.
Invariant curves: the flow $e^{tX}=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})$ preserves hyperbolas $uv=\text{const}$, the asymptotes of which are the two eigenlines.
In $SL(2,\mathbb R)$: $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}A=\tfrac12(2+\tfrac12)=\tfrac54>1$ → hyperbolic element, outside the classifying cone.
Shear parabolic type — only one eigen-direction

A horizontal slide whose amount depends on height:

$$ N = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad (u,v)\mapsto(u+v,\;v) $$

The height $v$ is completely frozen — $v$ maps to $v$. The horizontal position $u$ gains an extra $v$ — so the higher a point is, the further right it slides. Points on the $x$-axis ($v=0$) don't move at all.

Multiply out:

$$ Ne_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = e_1 \quad\checkmark\text{ fixed} $$

$e_1$ comes back exactly itself. The $x$-axis is the one eigenvector, with $\lambda=1$.

$$ Ne_2 = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} = e_1+e_2 $$

$e_2 = (0,1)^T$ does not come back parallel to itself. It lands at $(1,1)^T$ — it kept its height $1$ but picked up a horizontal shift of $1$. This is not a scaling: it is a mixing of the $y$-direction into the $x$-direction. That mixing is precisely what disqualifies $e_2$ from being an eigenvector.

An eigenvector must satisfy $Nv=\lambda v$ — output parallel to input. But $Ne_2=(1,1)^T$ is not parallel to $e_2=(0,1)^T$. So $e_2$ is not an eigenvector.

Powers accumulate linearly, not exponentially:

$$ N^k = \begin{bmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad e^{tN}=I+tN=\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}. $$

Because $N^2=0$ (the generator is nilpotent), the exponential series stops after one term. The shear parameter grows linearly with time — no exponential growth, no oscillation.

Area: $\det N = 1\cdot1-1\cdot0=1$. No scaling whatsoever, only sliding.

Faint circle = input. Solid ellipse = output (tilted). Orange arrow = $Ne_1=e_1$ (fixed); $Ne_2=e_1+e_2$ (slides right).
Complete picture
Eigenvalue: $\lambda=1$, repeated. Both "eigenvalues" are $1$, but there is only one independent eigenvector. This situation — repeated eigenvalue, deficient eigenvector space — is called a defective matrix.
Only one eigenvector: $e_1=(1,0)^T$. The $y$-direction has no independent eigen-line; it always mixes into the $x$-direction under $N$.
Why $N^2=0$: $N^2=\big[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\big]^2=\big[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\big]$ — wait, that is not zero! The generator $X$ with $e^{tN}=I+tX$ is $X=N-I=\big[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\big]$, and it is that trace-zero generator $X$ which satisfies $X^2=0$, not the group element $N$ itself.
What the unit circle does: becomes the tilted ellipse $(u-v)^2+v^2=1$. Area $=\pi$, unchanged.
In $SL(2,\mathbb R)$: $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}N=\tfrac12(1+1)=1$ → parabolic element, sitting exactly on the boundary of the classifying cone.

Side by side

Stretch Shear
Matrix $\operatorname{diag}(2,\,\tfrac12)$ $\big[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\big]$
Eigenvalues $\lambda_1=2,\;\lambda_2=\tfrac12$ (two distinct real) $\lambda=1$ (repeated, only one eigenvector)
Eigenvectors Two: $e_1$ and $e_2$ One: $e_1$ only
What it does Scales each axis independently Slides points horizontally by their height
det $1$ (stretch × shrink cancel) $1$ (no scaling at all)
Circle maps to Axis-aligned ellipse Tilted ellipse $(u-v)^2+v^2=1$
$\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}$ $\tfrac52>1$ → hyperbolic $1$ → parabolic (boundary)
In the cone Outside ($\det X<0$) On the cone ($\det X=0$)
The essential difference

A stretch has two independent eigen-directions — two axes each doing their own scaling. A shear has one: one axis stays put and everything else is dragged sideways. That single missing eigenvector is the whole story.
